title: Seeing the SQL
summary: ToQueryString and LogTo show you exactly what EF Core sends to the database.

steps.title: Never fly blind
body: EF Core writes SQL for you, but it is still SQL, and it still runs on a real database. Good EF Core developers look at it all the time. Two tools:
**`ToQueryString()`** turns a query into its SQL *without running it*:
The lambda parameter `b` became the table alias `"b"`. `Where` became `WHERE` and `OrderBy` became `ORDER BY`. Nothing happens in C#: the database does the filtering and the sorting.

steps.prompt: What is the last line this prints?
steps.explain: `OrderByDescending` becomes `ORDER BY ... DESC`, the last clause of the statement. There was no `EnsureCreated`: `ToQueryString` never touches the database.

steps.title: Logging every command
body: `ToQueryString` shows one query. To see **everything** a piece of code sends (inserts and updates too), turn on logging in `OnConfiguring`.
The simplest form prints every log message EF Core produces:

That is noisy, and each line includes a timing like `(3ms)` that changes on every run. In this course we use the overload that takes a **filter** and an **event**, and print only the SQL of each command that ran:
`RelationalEventId.CommandExecuted` fires once per SQL command, after it runs. The event data carries the `DbCommand`, whose `CommandText` is the SQL.

steps.prompt: This context logs every command as a line starting with `SQL>`. `Dojo.Capture` swallows what creating the database logs. What does the program print?
code: protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options
steps.explain: `EnsureCreated` sends commands too (`CREATE TABLE ...`), but `Dojo.Capture` hid them. What is left is the `INSERT`, with `RETURNING "Id"` so the generated key comes back, and the `SELECT`. Values travel as parameters (`@p0`, `@p1`), never pasted into the SQL. `Select(b => b.Title)` means only the `Title` column is read.

steps.prompt: Does the line send SQL to the database?
steps.explain: Queries run when they are enumerated or aggregated, and changes go out on `SaveChanges`. Building a query, tracking a new object and translating to text all stay in memory.

steps.prompt: Which of these sends a command to the database?
steps.explain: A query runs when you *enumerate* it: `ToList`, `First`, `Count`, a `foreach`. Building it with `Where` only describes it. `Add` only tracks, and `ToQueryString` only translates.

steps.prompt: Match the LINQ to the SQL it becomes.
steps.explain: Each operator maps to a clause. `Take` becomes `LIMIT` with a parameter, so the same SQL is reused for any page size.

steps.title: Show the query
prompt: The tests give you the `LibraryDb` from this lesson (`Books` with `Id`, `Title`, `Year`). Write

returning books published in or after 2000, ordered by `Title`. Return the **query**, not a list: the tests call `ToQueryString()` on it to check that the filtering and sorting happen in SQL, then run it.
template: dojoDb.Books.AddRange(new Book { Title = "Wolf Hall", Year = 2009 }, new Book { Title = "Emma", Year = 1815 },
new Book { Title = "Atonement", Year = 2001 }, new Book { Title = "Y2K", Year = 2000 });
Dojo.Check("filters in SQL (a WHERE clause)", dojoSql.Contains("WHERE"), dojoSql);
Dojo.Check("sorts in SQL (ORDER BY Title)", dojoSql.Contains("ORDER BY \"b\".\"Title\""), dojoSql);
Dojo.Eq("returns the right books", new List<string> { "Atonement", "Wolf Hall", "Y2K" }, Modern(dojoDb).Select(b => b.Title).ToList());

forbid.message: Returns a query, not a list
